title: Enzymes: effect of pH on amylase
aim: To investigate the effect of pH on the rate of reaction of the enzyme amylase, by timing how long it takes amylase to break down starch at different pH values.
background: Amylase is a carbohydrase enzyme made in the salivary glands and the pancreas. It catalyses the breakdown of starch into the sugar maltose. Iodine solution turns blue-black when starch is present and stays orange-brown when there is no starch, so it can be used to find out when all the starch has been broken down.

Enzymes have an active site with a specific shape that the substrate fits into. Each enzyme works best at a particular pH, called its optimum pH. If the pH is too far above or below the optimum, the bonds holding the enzyme's shape change, the active site changes shape, and the substrate no longer fits. The enzyme is then denatured and the rate of reaction falls.

In this practical, buffer solutions keep the pH of each reaction mixture constant. The time taken for the starch to disappear is measured, and the rate of reaction is calculated as rate = 1 ÷ time. A shorter time means a faster rate.
hypothesis: The rate of starch breakdown by amylase will be fastest at around pH 7 (the optimum pH) and will be slower at pH values above and below this, because the active site changes shape away from the optimum.

variables.independent: pH of the buffer solution (pH 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9).
variables.dependent: Time taken for the starch to be completely broken down (s), used to calculate rate of reaction (1 ÷ time).
control: Volume and concentration of amylase solution (2 cm³ of 1%)
Volume and concentration of starch solution (2 cm³ of 1%)
Number of drops of iodine in each well

equipment: Iodine solution in a dropping bottle
Electric water bath set to 35 °C (or a beaker of water and a Bunsen burner)
Test tubes and test tube rack
Syringes or measuring cylinders for measuring 1 cm³ and 2 cm³
method: Put one drop of iodine solution into each well of a spotting tile.
Set up a water bath at 35 °C and check the temperature with a thermometer.
Use a syringe to put 2 cm³ of amylase solution into a test tube, then add 1 cm³ of pH 4 buffer solution.
Use a different syringe to put 2 cm³ of starch solution into a second test tube.
Place both test tubes in the water bath for 5 minutes so the solutions reach 35 °C.
Pour the starch solution into the amylase and buffer mixture, mix with a pipette, and start the stopwatch immediately. Leave the tube in the water bath.
After 10 seconds, use a pipette to remove a drop of the mixture and add it to the first well of iodine. Return any excess to the test tube.
Repeat every 10 seconds, using the next well each time, until the iodine stays orange-brown (no blue-black colour). This shows that all the starch has been broken down.
Record the time at which the iodine first stays orange-brown. If the iodine is still blue-black after 300 seconds, record 'more than 300 s'.
Rinse the spotting tile and pipette, and repeat the whole procedure using each of the other buffers (pH 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9).
Repeat the investigation twice more at each pH and calculate the mean time.
Calculate the rate of reaction for each pH using rate = 1 ÷ mean time, and plot a graph of rate (y-axis) against pH (x-axis).

safety.risk: Irritates the eyes and stains skin.
safety.precaution: Wear eye protection and wash off any splashes on skin with water.

safety.risk: Enzymes can cause allergic reactions if they get on the skin or are inhaled.
safety.precaution: Avoid skin contact, wipe up spills immediately and wash hands after the practical.

safety.risk: Scalds from hot water if a Bunsen burner and beaker are used.
safety.precaution: Use an electric water bath set to 35 °C, or keep the Bunsen flame low and use tongs to handle hot apparatus.

safety.hazard: Buffer solutions (strongly acidic or alkaline buffers)
safety.precaution: Wear eye protection and use small volumes.

results.notes: Rate of reaction = 1 ÷ mean time, in s⁻¹, given to 3 significant figures. For example, at pH 7: 1 ÷ 30 = 0.0333 s⁻¹. Some students multiply by 1000 to give larger numbers (1000 ÷ time). Plot rate on the y-axis against pH on the x-axis and join the points with straight lines or a smooth curve.

analysis: The time taken for amylase to break down the starch was shortest at pH 7 (mean 30 s), so the rate of reaction was highest at pH 7 (0.0333 s⁻¹). The optimum pH for this amylase is about pH 7.
As the pH decreased from 7 to 4, the rate fell sharply, to 0.00345 s⁻¹ at pH 4. As the pH increased from 7 to 9, the rate also fell, to 0.00476 s⁻¹ at pH 9.

At pH values away from the optimum, the bonds holding the amylase molecule in shape are disrupted, so the shape of the active site changes. Fewer starch molecules fit into active sites, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form and the rate decreases. At extreme pH values the enzyme is denatured.
This fits with where amylase works in the body: in the mouth and small intestine, which are roughly neutral or slightly alkaline.

Because samples were taken only every 10 seconds, the true time could be up to 10 seconds less than the recorded time. The optimum could lie anywhere between pH 6 and pH 8; testing more pH values in this range (for example 6.5, 7.0, 7.5) would find it more precisely.

errors.error: Samples are only taken every 10 seconds, so the end point is only known to within 10 seconds.
errors.improvement: Sample more frequently (for example every 5 seconds), or use a colorimeter to measure the colour continuously.

errors.error: Deciding when the iodine is 'orange-brown' is subjective and different people may judge it differently.
errors.improvement: Compare each well with a control well of iodine plus water, and have the same person judge every end point.

errors.error: The temperature of the mixture may change while samples are being taken.
errors.improvement: Keep the test tube in a thermostatically controlled electric water bath throughout and check the temperature with a thermometer.

errors.error: Iodine from a previous well may be carried back into the reaction mixture by the pipette, or the pipette may carry over starch.
errors.improvement: Never touch the iodine with the pipette, and rinse the pipette with distilled water between samples.

examTips: Rate = 1 ÷ time. If the time is in seconds, the unit of rate is s⁻¹ (per second). Convert minutes to seconds before dividing.

Explain the effect of pH using the active site: away from the optimum the active site changes shape, the substrate no longer fits, fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form. Say 'denatured', never 'killed'.
Know why each step matters: buffer keeps pH constant, water bath keeps temperature constant, and solutions are pre-warmed so the reaction starts at the correct temperature.
The end point is when the iodine stays orange-brown, not when it turns blue-black.
Suggest testing more pH values close to the peak to find the optimum pH more precisely.

questions.question: In this practical, what does it show when a drop of the reaction mixture no longer turns the iodine blue-black?
options: All the starch has been broken down
The buffer has changed the pH
The maltose has been broken down into glucose
markScheme: 1 mark: there is no starch left / all the starch has been broken down (digested)
questions.explanation: Iodine only turns blue-black with starch. When it stays orange-brown, amylase has broken down all the starch into maltose. If amylase were denatured, starch would remain and the iodine would stay blue-black.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the mean time for starch to be broken down by amylase at pH 8.
Calculate the rate of reaction.
Use the equation:
rate = 1 ÷ time

headers: Mean time for starch to be broken down in s

questions.explanation: Rate = 1 ÷ 80 = 0.0125 per second. The unit is s⁻¹ because the time was measured in seconds.

questions.question:
A student repeated the investigation using a more dilute amylase solution.
At pH 5 the mean time for the starch to be broken down was 2 minutes 30 seconds.
Calculate the rate of reaction in s⁻¹.
Use the equation:
rate = 1 ÷ time
Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
markScheme: 1 mark: 2 minutes 30 seconds = 150 s
questions.explanation: Convert to seconds first: 2 × 60 + 30 = 150 s. Then rate = 1 ÷ 150 = 0.006666, which is 0.00667 s⁻¹ to 3 significant figures. Using 2.30 as the time is a common error.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the buffer solution in this investigation?
options: To provide the substrate for the enzyme
To stop the reaction at the end
To keep the pH of the reaction mixture at a fixed value
markScheme: 1 mark: to keep the pH constant (at a known value)
questions.explanation: A buffer resists changes in pH, so each reaction mixture stays at the pH being tested. The water bath controls temperature, and starch is the substrate.

questions.explanation: If cold solutions were mixed, the reaction would start at a lower temperature and run more slowly, giving times that reflect temperature as well as pH.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the results of an investigation into the effect of pH on amylase.
What is the best estimate of the optimum pH of this amylase?

headers: Mean time for starch to be broken down in s

markScheme: 1 mark: pH 7
questions.explanation: The optimum pH gives the fastest rate, which is the shortest time. pH 7 had the shortest time (30 s). Choosing pH 5 confuses the longest time with the fastest rate.

questions.question: Explain why amylase breaks down starch very slowly at pH 4.
acceptedAnswers: starch no longer fits active site
markScheme: 1 mark: pH 4 is far from the optimum pH (so bonds holding the enzyme's shape are disrupted)
1 mark: the shape of the active site changes / enzyme is denatured
1 mark: starch no longer fits the active site, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form
questions.explanation: Enzyme function depends on the shape of the active site. The acidic conditions alter that shape, so the substrate cannot bind. Avoid saying the enzyme is 'killed': enzymes are proteins, not living things.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows some results of an investigation into the effect of pH on amylase.
Calculate how many times faster the rate of reaction was at pH 7 than at pH 5.
Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

headers: Mean time for starch to be broken down in s

markScheme: 1 mark: rate at pH 7 = 1 ÷ 30 = 0.0333 s⁻¹ and rate at pH 5 = 1 ÷ 140 = 0.00714 s⁻¹
questions.explanation: Because rate = 1 ÷ time, the ratio of rates is the inverse ratio of the times: 140 ÷ 30 = 4.67, which is 4.7 to 2 significant figures.

acceptedAnswers: end point could be any time in the 30 s interval
markScheme: 1 mark: the starch may have been broken down at any time during the 30 s interval
1 mark: so the recorded time could be up to 30 s too long (less precise, harder to tell results apart)
questions.explanation: The sampling interval sets the resolution of the timing. With 30 s intervals, a reaction that took 35 s and one that took 55 s would both be recorded as 60 s.

questions.question: What is the product when amylase breaks down starch?
markScheme: 1 mark: maltose / sugars
questions.explanation: Amylase is a carbohydrase that breaks starch into maltose. Proteases produce amino acids, and lipases produce fatty acids and glycerol.

questions.question: Give two variables, other than temperature, that should be kept the same in an investigation into the effect of pH on amylase.
markScheme: 1 mark each, up to 2: volume or concentration of amylase; volume or concentration of starch; volume of buffer; time interval between samples; number of drops of iodine
questions.explanation: Each of these affects how quickly the starch disappears or how the end point looks, so only pH should be changed.

acceptedAnswers: test more pH values between 6 and 8
markScheme: 1 mark: use more pH values between pH 6 and pH 8 (smaller pH intervals, for example 6.5, 7.0, 7.5)
1 mark: repeat each and calculate means (or sample more frequently, for example every 5 s)
questions.explanation: With only whole-number pH values tested, the true optimum could be anywhere between 6 and 8. Testing closer values around the peak narrows down where the maximum rate is.

questions.question:
At pH 9 the rate of reaction was 0.00476 s⁻¹.
What was the mean time for the starch to be broken down?
Use the equation:
rate = 1 ÷ time
markScheme: 1 mark: 210 s
questions.explanation: Rearrange rate = 1 ÷ time to time = 1 ÷ rate = 1 ÷ 0.00476 = 210 s. The other options come from misreading the decimal place.

questions.question: Describe a method to investigate the effect of pH on the rate at which amylase breaks down starch.
markScheme: Indicative content: put drops of iodine in each well of a spotting tile; add a measured volume of amylase (2 cm³) and buffer of known pH (1 cm³) to a test tube; measured volume of starch (2 cm³) in another tube; place both in a water bath at a set temperature (for example 35 °C) for a few minutes; mix and start stopwatch; every 10 seconds add a drop of mixture to iodine; record time when iodine stays orange-brown; repeat for range of pH values (for example 4 to 9); repeat three times and calculate mean; calculate rate = 1 ÷ time; plot rate against pH; control variables: temperature, volumes and concentrations of amylase and starch, sampling interval

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, logically ordered method that would give valid results, including use of buffers, temperature control, sampling with iodine at regular intervals and how the end point is identified.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a method with most of the steps, but some detail is missing (for example how the end point is identified or how temperature is controlled).
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple, relevant statements such as mixing amylase and starch at different pH and testing with iodine, with little detail.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Top answers explain how pH is changed (buffers), how other variables are controlled (water bath, measured volumes), how the dependent variable is measured (sampling into iodine every 10 s) and what the end point is.

questions.question:
The results showed that the rate of reaction increased from pH 4 to pH 7 and then decreased from pH 7 to pH 9.
Explain this pattern.
markScheme: Indicative content: pH 7 is the optimum pH, where the active site has the right shape for starch to fit; maximum number of enzyme-substrate complexes form, so rate is highest; below and above the optimum, the pH alters the bonds holding the protein's shape; the active site changes shape; starch fits less well or not at all; fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form; rate decreases; at extreme pH the enzyme is denatured
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains both the rise and the fall using the idea of the optimum pH and the shape of the active site, with reference to enzyme-substrate complexes or denaturation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): describes the pattern or states that pH 7 is the optimum, with little explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Describing the pattern is not explaining it. The explanation must link pH to the shape of the active site and to how often starch can bind.
